# Green and facile method for the recovery of spent Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt Oxide (NMC) based Lithium ion batteries

Deepak Pant ⇑, Tenzin Dolker

a r t i c l e i n f o

Article history: Received 17 July 2016 Revised 25 September 2016 Accepted 26 September 2016 Available online xxxx

Keywords: Lithium ion batterie Citrus fruit Flavonoids Binder removal Counterion

## ABSTRACT

The research reports a novel green method to use citrus fruits for the management of spent NMC based lithium ion batteries (LIBs). Citrus fruit juice (CJ) can provide an excellent chemical combination to remove the binder and support the leaching with efficiency in between 94% to 100%. CJ have many advantages in LIBs recycling as an economic and green method due to rich in many organic acids like citric and malic acid as complexing agents with ascorbic acid and citrus flavonoids, for the reduction of many heavy metals. Application of CJ can avoid the use of N-Methylpyrrolidine, c-Butyrolactone, dimethylformamide, and dimethyl sulfoxide like toxic solvents commonly used for peeling off Al/Cu. Furthermore, counterions (like Na+, Mg ^+, Ca ^2+) present in CJ was responsible for the improvement in the leaching efficiency of organic acids. A mechanistic pattern of the overall reaction was also proposed and duly supported by various spectroscopic techniques. Binder removal experiment was supported by analytical techniques like XRD, XRF, IR, and FE-SEM, while the metal concentration was monitored by using ICP-MS analysis.  2016 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.

## 1. Introduction

Technological advancement has greatly increasing the demand for newer lithium ion batteries due to the more use of advanced energy storage devices like electric vehicles, consumer electronics, renewable energy storage, back-up power, medical devices, etc. It was reported that in the year 2006 rechargeable (secondary) batteries covered 11% of the total global battery business and it was growing at the rate of 6% annually (Battery Statistics, 2015). India is the world’s second-largest cellular phone user with over 930.20 million subscribers (547.70 million urban and 382.50 million rural) as on November 2014 (TRAI, 2014).

The removal of the binder is an essential step towards the recovery of metals from spent lithium ion batteries. It can be removed either by the high temperature treatment (Guo et al., 2016) or by using solvents like N-methyl pyrrolidone (NMP), c-Butyrolactone, dimethylformamide, and dimethyl sulfoxide (Li et al., 2013, 2010a). High-temperature treatment process required temperature 500–700 C and has many issues related to toxic emission and material management (Wang et al., 2016), whereas solvents based techniques have the limitation in terms of toxicity and post management (Chen and Zhou, 2014). So some alternative technique is the need of the hour.

The existing methods for metal recovery from LIB recycling involved: (i) aqueous stream based limited recycling using the liquid stream mixed with soda ash with the hammer mill and shaker table (Meshram et al., 2015a); (ii) supercritical CO2 based recycling of cathode and anode (Bertuol et al., 2016) (iii) pyro and hydrometallurgical processes (Chen et al., 2015a; Pant and Singh, 2014). There was also some limitation over pyro-metallurgical processes towards the recovery of lithium and aluminium and further treatment is needed for the recovery of Li (Hanisch et al., 2015).

The use of strong acids can provide good results in metal leaching but harmful emission like Cl2, S 0x and NOx makes its limitation to be a popular technique, also the post management of acids is a complex issue (Zhang et al., 2013). Organic acid has the potential to avoid these adverse environmental impacts. Pure citric, oxalic malic, aspartic, ascorbic, tartaric and iminodiacetic acids (Sun and Qiu, 2012; Li et al., 2013; Nayaka et al., 2015b) can be used as the leaching agent for LIB recycling with incomplete leaching. Use of pure organic acid cannot provide efficient leaching and for improvement H2O2 (1–6 vol.%) be used as a reducing agent (L et al., 2010b).

To avoids the use of H2O2 like toxicant methods can be modified by using mixture of acids (Table 1) out of which one acid is used as a complexing agent and another as a reducing agent (Li et al., 2012; Nayaka et al., 2016). Citric and malic acid with a different combination of ascorbic acid/ H2O2 give nearly 100% leaching of Li (Nayaka et al., 2015a; Li et al., 2013). Cobalt gives average leaching in between 60% and 97% and best results are with the combination of malic acid and ascorbic acid (Nayaka et al., 2015b).

[TABLE:TABLE_Green and Facile Method for the Recovery of Spent Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt Oxide (NMC) Based Lithium Ion Batteries_0001]

To develop more environmentally benign process, i.e. avoid the use of H2O2 and mineral acid like toxicant; in an affordable cost we are proposing the use of CJ as a green solvent. Waste resultant from LIBs can cause an inescapable risk for the environment and public health (Pant et al., 2012), while on the other hand it have the harm to improper dispose to the metal resources like Li, Co, Ni and Mn. In year 2005 cobalt in LIB waste was found 12,000 tonnes and respective to this the approximate amount for Li, Mn and Ni contents were 5723, 35,312 and 21,970, respectively (Dewulf et al., 2010). A proper management strategic can reduce the risk of the release of toxic organic compound and also mitigate the risk of resource depletion. The use of CJ for the recovery of metals from waste LIB can make the process safe for the environment with an effective recovery. CJ is a source of mixed organic acid with flavonoids as complexing and reducing agent with different counterions for efficient leaching and binder removal. This study will devote to discover a green recovery of Li, Co, Ni and Mn from LIB using CJ as the innovative waste management.

## 2. Experimental

For the metal recovery from waste LIBs of mobile phones (collected from the local scrap market) these were discharge first and then dismantled to separate the cathode and anode film (Scheme 1). Hill lemon, galgal (Citrus pseudolimon Tanaka), a cheap fruit commonly present in a Himachal Pradesh with good quantity, is used for the present study as CJ material. Galgal is light yellow, conical ovate with prominent ridges and smooth surface fruit growing in subhumid-subtropical areas in the upper Shivalik ranges of Himachal Pradesh. It is a member of the citrus family, and due to heavy pulp it has some limited applications. The average fruit weight was around 400–500 g with diameter 10–11.5 cm. The total acid concentration in the CJ was measured by alkaline titration method (Manly et al., 1972) and was found 52,600 mg/L. Individual acid concentration was measured by using reverse phase HPLC, using 250 mm 4.6 mm i.d., 5 lm particle Hypersil Gold aQ Analytical Column. The detector was set at λ= 254 nm for ascorbic acid and k = 214 nm for the other organic acids. The concentration of citric acid, malic acid, and ascorbic acid present in above CJ were 50,300, 1500 and 230 mg/L, respectively. Commonly present flavonoids in CJ were quercetin, myricitin, rutin, tangeritin, naringin and hesperidin (Okwu, 2008).

[TABLE:TABLE_Green and Facile Method for the Recovery of Spent Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt Oxide (NMC) Based Lithium Ion Batteries_0002]

## 2.1. Binder removal and leaching

Binder removal experiments were carried out in batch mode using the 250 mL round-bottom flask with a temperature controlling facility. The flask was equipped with a magnetic stirrer for homogenization. Experiments were performed by using CJ with cathode and anode film. Optimum w/v ratio of film to CJ was found to be 50,000 mg/L at 90 ^∘C and 20 min for binder removal. Cu (anode) and Al (cathode) film were separate, washed with water and check its purity using XRD and XRF techniques. After the removal of Cu and Al the remaining solution was refluxed for 30 min and then filter to remove carbon and other impurities. The filtrate was used to check the leaching rate, using Eq. (2.1). Leaching rate is the percentage ratio of the amount of metal species in the leachate to the total amount, as measured by tri-acid digestion process (Uppsala, 2015) using ICP-MS.

## 2.2. Analytical methods

X-ray diffractometer (Rigaku, Cu-K) and XRF (Elvax – Elvatech) were used for the qualitative detection of metals. IR spectroscopy (Bruker) was used to confirm the binder removal and change in ligand environment during the experiment. FE-SEM (JSM-7600F) technique was used to check the surface morphology during the experiments. Thermo Scientific, ELEMENT XR, high performance, double focusing magnetic sector field ICP-MS was used for quantitative measurement of metals. pH was measured by using the Flucka Digital pH meter and chemicals used are of AR grade.

## 3. Results and discussion

## 3.1. Binder removal and recovery of Al and Cu

A typical X-ray diffractogram of cathodes of spent Li-ion batteries before and after treatment was shown in Fig. 1. LiCoO2, Co3O4, Al and carbon were found in the cathode samples as compared with previous reports and JCPDS standards (Freitas et al., 2010).

[TABLE:TABLE_Green and Facile Method for the Recovery of Spent Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt Oxide (NMC) Based Lithium Ion Batteries_0003]

The presence of Co3O4 and LiCoO2 resultant from the reaction was due to the charging–discharging cycles. The role of carbon in both cathode and anode was to increase electric conductivity of the electrode (Contestabile et al., 2001; Lain, 2001). 2h scattering of Al at 37.791 with intensity 14.005 counts was shifted to 38.372 and 27.544 counts after the binder removal. Some other 2h patterns and intensity 78.681, 11.091 were also got shifted to 78.277, 14.787. It may be due to the resultant defects (Cuesta et al., 1998) after the binder removal.

In the XRD and XRF pattern of the anode (Figs. 2a and 2b) showed the presence of carbon as an active material and Cu as a current collector. Cu shows 2h diffraction pattern at 43.142, 54.5 and 73.986. XRF pattern clearly shows the Cu recovery after binder removal as initial Cu Ka at 72,000 was crossed to 100,000 counts. FESEM images (Fig. 3) presents the microstructural changes on the cathode and anode film during treatment. It was found that the removal was initiated through the cracks. In FTIR PVDF gives characteristic strong absorption due to the fluorocarbon group at (Fig. 4) 1194 and 866 c̅ ̅m̅ ^-1, these bonds were shifted to 1174 and 860 in the cathode film due to the possible involvement of fluoro group in the coating. The absorption due to fluoro group was found to be completely removed after the treatment of film for 20 min at 90 ^∘𝖢. The same pattern was also reflected in FTIR of the anode. The binder removal rate was quantitatively measured by using Eq. (3.1) and was found 8% and 9.6% in case of anode and cathode. For this purpose average weight loss of 10 films from cathode and anode were noted before and after treatment.

% Removal Rate = ((A - B) / n) / (A) x100. (Eq. 3.1)

where A is the average weight of film before treatment, B is average weight of film after treatment, and n is total number of films.

## 3.2. Leaching of Li, Co, Mn and Ni

After the removal of Cu and Al the remaining solution contains Li, Co, Mn and Ni as the main elements (From XRD and XRF investigation). The solution was further refluxed for 30 min at 90 ^∘C to ensure the maximum leaching. The leachate was then separated by filtration and filtrate was analyzed through ICP-MS. Li, Co, Mn and Ni concentration varies in different brands of LIBs waste and broadly in the range of 4224 to 3065 for Li, 8756 to 4822 for Γ0, 28,368 to 19,470 for Mn, 3843 to 2514 ppm for Ni as found in 05 popular brands Nokia, Samsung, Lava, Sony and Max. The leaching efficiency of the various metals was found as 100 for lithium, 99% for Mn, 98% Ni and 94% for Co. Minimum leaching efficiency of Co showed its minimum reduction under reaction condition.

In the mixed oxides leaching, reducing agent always play an important role in improving leaching efficiency (Dorella and Mansur, 2007; Ferreira et al., 2009; Nayl et al., 2014). It was reported that reducing agent significantly improve the leaching efficiency of citric, malic, oxalic and aspartic acid (Li et al., 2014; Sun and Qiu, 2012) in the LIB recycling by reducing different metals in their lower oxidation stage. CJ consists of the mixture ofa various complexing agent like citric and malic acid with ascorbic acid and flavonoids were used as reducing agents (Rekha et al., 2012; Sierra et al., 2016). The presence of various counterions for citrate and malate anions like Ca^2+, Na+, K+ were found to improve the complexation. Mechanistically the role of counterions can be explained

by the pH metric and its correlation with electrochemical behaviour. The pH of the leachate was found 5.9 in the case ofjuice, whereas 2.4 and 1.9 in the case of individual citric and malic acid. It indicates more existence of citric and malic complex as compared to hydroxide for improved leaching (Table 2). This finding was well evidenced with some of the previous studies as the addition of sodium citrate in citric acid improved the leaching pattern and it results the 2–3 points increment in pH. Hydroxides were formed at lower (acidic) pH responsible for incomplete leacing and more precipitation, where metal acid complexes are responsible for improved leaching (Mehrizi et al., 2013).

Acid flavonoids can be reasonably used as an environmentally benign weak reducing agent, similar to some metal oxide dissolution studies (Manjanna et al., 2001). Fig. 6 shows the initial and final (after 60 min, 90 C with LIB) IR spectra of juice. Compared with the spectra of pure citric and malic acid it shows the complexation pattern ofjuice during the course of the reaction. The absorption due to C CO asymmetric peak in the range of 1527 cm1 was more intense in the final complex. Absorption at 1694 cm ^-1 in the final product was due to the appearance of COO vibrational bond indicating complexation and pi interaction within the metals-metal and metal-ligand (Tsimbler et al., 1969).

The overall leaching reaction involving the following parallel steps (Fig. 5): (i) reduction of Co(III), Mn (IV) and Ni (III) to Co(II), Mn (II) and Ni (II) in the presence of ascorbic acid and citrus flavonoids, resultant the dissolution of spent LiXO2; (ii) more formation of metal acid complexes in the presence of counter ions for less precipitation and more dissolution, and finally (iii) recovery of

metals from leachant solution using Ν4 ⊂O3 and Oxalic acid (Meshram et al., 2015b).

## 4. Conclusion

CJ was found to be a good reagent for the metal recycling from the waste LIBs. It plays a good role in removing the binder and provides an efficient leaching for LIB waste with an excellent combination of reducing agents and counterions. Furthermore:

1. The XRD pattern in cathode clearly shows an increment in intensity from 14.005 counts to 38.372 due to the removing defects in the material in case of binder removal;

2. In the FTIR absorption due to fluorocarbon group at 1194 and 866 cm ^-1 was completely removed due to removal in fluorocarbon bonding;

3. Ascorbic acid and flavonoids were found as reducing agent for metal leaching;

4. Ca^2+, Na+, K+ like counterions can support leaching by avoiding the formation of metal hydroxide.

This study will provide a new direction towards the use of CJ as a new green reagent for metal recycling from different sources including E-waste.

## 2.1. Binder removal and leaching
Binder removal experiments were carried out in batch mode using the 250 mL round-bottom flask with a temperature controlling facility. The flask was equipped with a magnetic stirrer for homogenization. Experiments were performed by using CJ with cathode and anode film. Optimum w/v ratio of film to CJ was found to be 50,000 mg/L at 90 ^∘C and 20 min for binder removal. Cu (anode) and Al (cathode) film were separate, washed with water and check its purity using XRD and XRF techniques. After the removal of Cu and Al the remaining solution was refluxed for 30 min and then filter to remove carbon and other impurities. The filtrate was used to check the leaching rate, using Eq. (2.1). Leaching rate is the percentage ratio of the amount of metal species in the leachate to the total amount, as measured by tri-acid digestion process (Uppsala, 2015) using ICP-MS.

text_chunk.text:
## 3. Results and discussion
## 3.1. Binder removal and recovery of Al and Cu
A typical X-ray diffractogram of cathodes of spent Li-ion batteries before and after treatment was shown in Fig. 1. LiCoO2, Co3O4, Al and carbon were found in the cathode samples as compared with previous reports and JCPDS standards (Freitas et al., 2010).
The presence of Co3O4 and LiCoO2 resultant from the reaction was due to the charging–discharging cycles. The role of carbon in both cathode and anode was to increase electric conductivity of the electrode (Contestabile et al., 2001; Lain, 2001). 2h scattering of Al at 37.791 with intensity 14.005 counts was shifted to 38.372 and 27.544 counts after the binder removal. Some other 2h patterns and intensity 78.681, 11.091 were also got shifted to 78.277, 14.787. It may be due to the resultant defects (Cuesta et al., 1998) after the binder removal.
In the XRD and XRF pattern of the anode (Figs. 2a and 2b) showed the presence of carbon as an active material and Cu as a current collector. Cu shows 2h diffraction pattern at 43.142, 54.5 and 73.986. XRF pattern clearly shows the Cu recovery after binder removal as initial Cu Ka at 72,000 was crossed to 100,000 counts. FESEM images (Fig. 3) presents the microstructural changes on the cathode and anode film during treatment. It was found that the removal was initiated through the cracks. In FTIR PVDF gives characteristic strong absorption due to the fluorocarbon group at (Fig. 4) 1194 and 866 c̅ ̅m̅ ^-1, these bonds were shifted to 1174 and 860 in the cathode film due to the possible involvement of fluoro group in the coating. The absorption due to fluoro group was found to be completely removed after the treatment of film for 20 min at 90 ^∘𝖢. The same pattern was also reflected in FTIR of the anode. The binder removal rate was quantitatively measured by using Eq. (3.1) and was found 8% and 9.6% in case of anode and cathode. For this purpose average weight loss of 10 films from cathode and anode were noted before and after treatment.
% Removal Rate = ((A - B) / n) / (A) x100. (Eq. 3.1) where A is the average weight of film before treatment, B is average weight of film after treatment, and n is total number of films.

text_chunk.text:
## 3.2. Leaching of Li, Co, Mn and Ni
After the removal of Cu and Al the remaining solution contains Li, Co, Mn and Ni as the main elements (From XRD and XRF investigation). The solution was further refluxed for 30 min at 90 ^∘C to ensure the maximum leaching. The leachate was then separated by filtration and filtrate was analyzed through ICP-MS. Li, Co, Mn and Ni concentration varies in different brands of LIBs waste and broadly in the range of 4224 to 3065 for Li, 8756 to 4822 for Γ0, 28,368 to 19,470 for Mn, 3843 to 2514 ppm for Ni as found in 05 popular brands Nokia, Samsung, Lava, Sony and Max. The leaching efficiency of the various metals was found as 100 for lithium, 99% for Mn, 98% Ni and 94% for Co. Minimum leaching efficiency of Co showed its minimum reduction under reaction condition.
In the mixed oxides leaching, reducing agent always play an important role in improving leaching efficiency (Dorella and Mansur, 2007; Ferreira et al., 2009; Nayl et al., 2014). It was reported that reducing agent significantly improve the leaching efficiency of citric, malic, oxalic and aspartic acid (Li et al., 2014; Sun and Qiu, 2012) in the LIB recycling by reducing different metals in their lower oxidation stage. CJ consists of the mixture ofa various complexing agent like citric and malic acid with ascorbic acid and flavonoids were used as reducing agents (Rekha et al., 2012; Sierra et al., 2016). The presence of various counterions for citrate and malate anions like Ca^2+, Na+, K+ were found to improve the complexation. Mechanistically the role of counterions can be explained
D. Pant, T. Dolker/Waste Management xxx (2016) xxx–xxx by the pH metric and its correlation with electrochemical behaviour. The pH of the leachate was found 5.9 in the case ofjuice, whereas 2.4 and 1.9 in the case of individual citric and malic acid. It indicates more existence of citric and malic complex as compared to hydroxide for improved leaching (Table 2). This finding was well evidenced with some of the previous studies as the addition of sodium citrate in citric acid improved the leaching pattern and it results the 2–3 points increment in pH. Hydroxides were formed at lower (acidic) pH responsible for incomplete leacing and more precipitation, where metal acid complexes are responsible for improved leaching (Mehrizi et al., 2013).
Acid flavonoids can be reasonably used as an environmentally benign weak reducing agent, similar to some metal oxide dissolution studies (Manjanna et al., 2001). Fig. 6 shows the initial and final (after 60 min, 90 C with LIB) IR spectra of juice. Compared with the spectra of pure citric and malic acid it shows the complexation pattern ofjuice during the course of the reaction. The absorption due to C CO asymmetric peak in the range of 1527 cm1 was more intense in the final complex. Absorption at 1694 cm ^-1 in the final product was due to the appearance of COO vibrational bond indicating complexation and pi interaction within the metals-metal and metal-ligand (Tsimbler et al., 1969).
The overall leaching reaction involving the following parallel steps (Fig. 5): (i) reduction of Co(III), Mn (IV) and Ni (III) to Co(II), Mn (II) and Ni (II) in the presence of ascorbic acid and citrus flavonoids, resultant the dissolution of spent LiXO2; (ii) more formation of metal acid complexes in the presence of counter ions for less precipitation and more dissolution, and finally (iii) recovery of

final.content: Cathode and anode films from waste mobile phone LIBs were treated with Citrus pseudolimon (galgal) juice in a 250 mL round-bottom flask at a film-to-juice w/v ratio of 50,000 mg/L, 90 °C for 20 min for binder removal; after separating Cu and Al films, the remaining solution was refluxed for 30 min and filtered to remove carbon and impurities, and the filtrate was analyzed for leaching rate by ICP-MS relative to tri-acid digestion.
final.evidence_span: Cathode and anode films from waste mobile phone LIBs were treated with Citrus pseudolimon (galgal) juice in a 250 mL round-bottom flask at a film-to-juice w/v ratio of 50,000 mg/L, 90 °C for 20 min for binder removal; after separating Cu and Al films, the remaining solution was refluxed for 30 min and filtered to remove carbon and impurities, and the filtrate was analyzed for leaching rate by ICP-MS relative to tri-acid digestion.
